nameStory: This little crab gets its name from its incredible partnership with Sargassum seaweed, where it spends its entire life floating in the open ocean. The "swimming" part comes from its flattened back legs that work like paddles, helping it navigate through the floating seaweed mats. It was named after Thomas Say, one of America's pioneering naturalists who helped describe many of our native species.
description: The Sargassum Swimming Crab is a small, colorful ocean wanderer that lives its entire life floating among mats of Sargassum seaweed in the open Atlantic. Unlike the crabs you might find scuttling along the beach, this one is perfectly adapted for life in the water column, with paddle-like back legs for swimming. Its body is typically brownish-yellow with intricate patterns that help it blend perfectly with the seaweed it calls home. These crabs are quite small, usually no bigger than a silver dollar.

idTips.label: Paddle-shaped back legs
idTips.description: The last pair of legs are flattened into oval paddles instead of pointed claws - feel how they're wider and thinner than a typical crab's legs

idTips.label: Mottled coloration
idTips.description: Body shows intricate brown, yellow, and sometimes blue patterns that perfectly mimic floating Sargassum seaweed

idTips.label: Small, lightweight build
idTips.description: Feels surprisingly light in your hand compared to similar-sized shore crabs, with a relatively flat, streamlined body

idTips.label: Sharp front claws
idTips.description: Front pincers are notably sharp and well-developed for grasping onto seaweed and catching small prey

idTips.label: Found with Sargassum
idTips.description: Almost always discovered clinging to or moving through floating brown Sargassum seaweed mats

habitat: In New England waters, you'll encounter these crabs only when floating mats of Sargassum seaweed wash close to shore or beach themselves after storms. They live in the open ocean, so finding one usually means the Gulf Stream or warm ocean currents have brought their seaweed home northward. Look for them in tide pools or stranded seaweed after strong onshore winds or tropical storms.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen, as warm ocean currents haven't yet brought Sargassum mats close to New England shores.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to spot them when Gulf Stream eddies or warm water masses bring floating Sargassum close to shore or onto beaches.
seasonality.fall: Hurricane season may wash Sargassum mats and their crab inhabitants onto New England beaches, especially after tropical storms.
seasonality.winter: Virtually absent, as cold water temperatures and offshore currents keep their Sargassum habitat far from New England.

funFact: These crabs are essentially ocean nomads that never touch the sea bottom - they're born, live, mate, and die while drifting thousands of miles across the Atlantic in their floating seaweed cities, making them true citizens of the open sea.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with juvenile blue crabs, but the Sargassum Swimming Crab's paddle-shaped back legs are the dead giveaway - remember "paddles for the pelagic wanderer" while blue crabs have pointed walking legs.
contextualKnowledge: Since these crabs live in tropical and subtropical waters, finding one in New England is actually quite special - it means you're seeing a traveler from warmer seas who made an epic journey north with the ocean currents.
compareHints: While it's the only Portunus species regularly found in New England, it differs from other swimming crabs in the family by its smaller size and exclusive association with floating Sargassum. Other swimming crabs like blue crabs are much larger and live on the sea bottom rather than in floating seaweed. The paddle-shaped swimming legs are shared with other portunid crabs, but the Sargassum Swimming Crab's pelagic lifestyle and seaweed camouflage are unique.
